title: A geometrically maximal torus in a reductive group is its own scheme-theoretic centralizer
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] with algebraic closure $\bar k$. All group schemes are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroup schemes are closed [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness is as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], and connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]; geometrically connected means connected after extension to $\bar k$. A torus is a group scheme $T$ such that $T_{\bar k}\simeq(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m$ is as in [def-sc-gm-ga]. A maximal torus in a group scheme is a torus subgroup not strictly contained in another torus subgroup. A smooth affine group is unipotent if in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation every geometric point $u$ satisfies $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. A smooth geometrically connected group $G$ is reductive if $G_{\bar k}$ has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup scheme. Let $G$ be reductive and let $T\subseteq G$ be a torus such that $T_{\bar k}$ is maximal in $G_{\bar k}$. For a commutative $k$-algebra $A$, define $C_G(T)(A)$ to consist of the elements $g\in G(A)$ whose image commutes with every element of $T(A')$ in $G(A')$ for every commutative $A$-algebra $A'$. Then the subgroup functor $C_G(T)$ equals $T$; in particular it is represented by the closed subgroup scheme $T\subseteq G$. The equality is scheme-theoretic, including on nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Proposition 17.61(a), printed p.372; centralizer functor as in Proposition 1.92, printed pp.33--34. Only the self-centralizer assertion (a) is used, not the centre containment assertion (b).

proof.text: Write $G=\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $T=\operatorname{Spec}D$. The affine morphism correspondence [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-into-affine-scheme] and tensor-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product] give $G\times G=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$. Its diagonal is closed because multiplication $R\otimes_kR\to R$ is surjective [def-weil-closed-immersion]. The same diagonal calculation for $R$ and $D$ checks separatedness of $G$ and $T$; finite sets of algebra generators check finite type for the product [def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-weil-proper-morphism]. Apply [lem-sfb-constant-source-closed-factorization-locus] with $Y=T$, $S=G$, $X=G\times G$, $W=\Delta_G$, and $f(t,g)=(t,gtg^{-1})$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. It gives a closed subscheme $C\subseteq G$. For $g:\operatorname{Spec}A\to G$, factorization through $C$ says conjugation by $g$ fixes $T_A$. This is exactly the all-$A\prime$ condition: the reverse implication is tested on the universal point over $A\otimes_kD$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Products and inverses of elements centralizing all $T(A\prime)$ again centralize them, so $C$ is a subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. The base-change clause, applied to $G_K\to G$, identifies $C_K=C_{G_K}(T_K)$ for every field extension $K/k$: $T\times_kS\prime=T_K\times_KS\prime$ for any $K$-scheme $S\prime$.

source.place: Proposition 1.92 and following paragraph, printed pp.33--34; explicit application of the existing factorization-locus theorem.

proof.text: Put $K=\bar k$, $H=G_K$, $S=T_K$ and $C_K=C_H(S)$ by step 1. The base-change assertion (2) of [lem-pc-proper-base-change] makes $H$ smooth. The hypotheses give that $H$ is connected with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup, and that $S$ is maximal. By [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], $C_K$ is smooth and connected; by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced] it is reduced. For every Borel $B$ containing $S$, [lem-sfb-maximal-torus-centralizer-borel] gives $C_K\subseteq B$, hence $C_K\subseteq I=\bigcap_{B\supseteq S}B$.

source.place: Proposition 17.61(a), printed p.372, first sentence and containment; Corollary 13.10 and Theorem 17.38.

proof.text: The image of the connected scheme $C_K$ in $I$ is connected and contains the identity, so lies in its identity component [def-weil-connected-scheme]. Its map factors through the reduced closed subscheme supported there: any element of the defining radical ideal pulls back into every prime ideal of the reduced coordinate ring $K[C_K]$, hence is zero [def-weil-pbc-scheme-reduction]. Thus $C_K\subseteq(I_{\mathrm{red}})^\circ$. By [lem-sfb-chevalley-borel-intersection] the latter is $R_u(H)\cdot S$. Since $R_u(H)$ is smooth connected normal unipotent and $H$ is reductive, $R_u(H)=1$ by the hypothesis, and its product with $S$ is $S$. We obtain $C_K\subseteq S$. Conversely $S$ is a split product of copies of $\mathbf G_m$, so its points commute over every algebra [def-sc-gm-ga], giving $S\subseteq C_K$. Consequently $C_K=S$ as closed subgroup schemes, not only on field points.

source.place: Proposition 17.61(a), printed p.372, displayed chain using Theorem 17.56; reduction/component factorization written explicitly.

proof.text: Let $J_C,J_T\subseteq R$ be the defining ideals of $C,T\subseteq G$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Step 1 and $C_K=T_K$ give $J_C(R\otimes_kK)=J_T(R\otimes_kK)$. For every $k$-vector space $V$, the map $V\to V\otimes_kK$, $v\mapsto v\otimes1$, is injective: for $v\ne0$ extend $v$ to a basis and take the coefficient functional sending $v$ to $1$. Applied to $V=R/J_T$ and then $R/J_C$, this implies $J_C\subseteq J_T$ and $J_T\subseteq J_C$. Thus $C=T$ over $k$. The representing closed subschemes are equal, so their functors agree on every commutative $k$-algebra, including nonreduced ones.
